results.title: THE CROCODILE PITS OF MAABDEH. (Evening Post, 12 January 1895)
results.fulltext: the crocodile pits of maabdeh on the east bdo of the nile arid at some little distance from the river are some of the most ancient mummy pits of ancient egypt they consist of large chambers hewn out of the bolid rock by the hands of nature inti which the ancient inhabitants of the nile valley have deposited tinmortal remains of the sacred crocodiles each chamber is a bout from thirty to forty feet wide but only about three to four feet in height on entering these pits we are able to proceed in an upright posture for some considerable time but finally are bound to go down on our hands and knees if it is our intention to enter the chambers eacred to the holy dead the sight that meets the eye of the explorer as he looks round him aided only by the dim light of his candle is probably one of the most ghastly that can be imagined on all sides are the remains of men women and children in various positions some are lying at full length on their backs while others are standing up against the wall as if to ask the intruder his reasons for disturbing their long rest logs and arms of mummies which have been torn to pieces by the arabs in search of treasure are scattered the floor on all sides the main feature of the pits maabdeh is the enormous number of crocodiles with which the various chambers are filled the animals are arranged head to tail and tail to head as closely as it is possible for them to be packed and around them are their little one in almost countless numbers how many crocodile mummies there really are in these pits it is difficult to say but considering that they are placed one upon the other and taking also into consideration that the worship of the crocodile or sut as the egyptians called it was very ancient it is probable that the antiquity and great value

red and white linen the heads covered by masks representing the cat and made of the same linen there have been more mummies of the ibis found in egypt than of any other bird or animal but very few in hardly ever have mummied animals been discovered in the human tombs and never by any chance were amulets put with animals crocodiles were embalmed and deposited in catacombs purposely excavated for carefully done and the cloth was of a red colour in addition to the usual yellow-stained linen in addition to fiese numrous small fishes have been discovered and yet smaller insects all carefully embalmed and deposited in the several tombs prepared to receive them in many cases the animals were placed in mummy pots in others simply bandaged and laid in the pits and in only a few instances have results.title: THE MANUFACTURE OF MUMMIES. (Auckland Star, 10 December 1902)
results.fulltext: the manufacture of mummies mummy restoration is the newest of the arts having been invented recently by a scientist connected with the american museum of natural history in jntew york by the aid of a simple yet ingenious process it brings back the ancient dead to the aspect of life or something near it giving them the appearance they had hundreds or even thousands of years ago mummification consists of course in the withdrawal of all water from the tissues of the body which is thus reduced to absolute dryness it follows then that if the water can be putback into the flesh and parchment-like skin the desiccated individual will be restored to something like his original appearance this is exactly what is accomplished by the process referred to the desiccation is so absolute that the body of a man who weighed perhaps iso pounds in jife is likely to tip the scales at not more than fourteen pounds all of the tissues being extremely shrunken while the parchment-like skin holds the bones like a bag as a rule the hair is well preserved and in many instances the eyes are quite perfect yet in many cases doubtless the mummies are thousands of years old the process of restoration consists in placing the munimj in ai box and introducing water vapour in the shape of comparatively cool steam it has to be done gradually but when properly applied the vapour is slowly absorbed the dried body finally assuming the contour of life from a scientific standpoint the achievement is most interesting inasmuch as the ethnologist is enabled to ascertain what these mummied people looked like when they were alive i when thus restored the mummies become liable to decay and for that reason they are preserved in alcohol the manufacture of artificial mummies a very different process from the foregoing has recently become quite a profitable industry out of a consignment of twenty-one mummies shipped not long ago froim egypt to an institution in america by a well-known archaeologist nineteen were found to be frauds skeletons obtained by professional ghoula from modern graveyards are wrapped in a kind of cloth resembling in appearance the mummy-cloth of the ancient egyptians the wrapping is done with the help of modern glue and when the mummy is finished it is placed in a counterfeit mummy-coffin of papier mache mummy-coffins of this kind are being turned out by hundreds in paris painted from egyptian originals with the curious and complicated figures and inscriptions customarily applied to such boxes for the dead in the days of the pharaohs finally the imitation mummies enclosed in the bogus cases are shipped to egypt where they are sold to tourists at profitable rates a mummy in good condition is worth from 15 to 100 it is a curious fact that frauds in mummies were commonly practised in ancient egypt all of the business of mummy-making was in the hands of the priests and it was part of their work to preserve in this way the bodies of sacred animals such as cats crocodiles and ibises frequently however they preferred to do up a bundle of rags and palm it off as the mummy of a monkey or an ibis getting their pay just the same doubtless so common was this practice that nowadays mummies of animals received from egypt are x-rayed before taking the trouble to unwrap them fake mummies are by no means unknown in america only a short time ago the alleged mummy of a nine-foot giant turned up in atlanta having been found so the showman said who owed it in california it was so excellently made as to deceive some expert archaeologists and the fact that it was counterfeit might never biave been discovered had it not been that the proprietor was arrested for debt meanwhile mr f a lucas of thcs smithsonian institution had been sent to atlanta to investigate the matter and finding the giant ia pawn he was able to dissect it partly as a result it was ascertained that the mummy was composed chiefly of gunny sacking and iron pipe another alleged mummy whicli had been exhibited with the giant represented a child in the top of whose head was sticking a stone axe it was supposed to represent a very ancient murder but on investigation proved to consist mainly of unsized paper which had been treated with ttfiin glue water to make it look like human sldn the upper lip was drawn up to show the incisor teeth which had belonged originally to a cow and the hair was of jute altogether it was a most ingenious fake one side of the body being caved in to show two ribs when these mummies were seized for debt the lawyer for the bankrupt showman pleaded on behalf of ms eiient that it was contrary to laf to attach a corpse but the discovery that the objects in question were not really mummies at all but only imitations altered the aspect of the case as to what eventually became of the fakes nobody seenia ix know but it is likely that ftiq m ecdubsikaa somewhere noww jj

results.fulltext: cats the veneration of sacred animals was a form of religious worship peculiar to the egyptians and held such a place in the national religion that it excited the greatest attention even in ancient times besides the apis bulls in memphis who possessed their own palace and a magnificent sepulchre cows cats the ibis sparrow-hawk dogs crocodiles and many other animals received divine veneration whoever intentionally killed a sacred animal was punished with death we know that the egyptians excelled in the art of embalming and treated not only their relations but the sacred animals to this process consideration of this matter takes us back to the time bc and it comes like a shock to read the following almost sacriligeous act taken from a home paper prom egypt there have been imported several large consignments of mummy cats for fertilising use in agriculture one day at the rooms of gordon co a coincidence in the names liverpool no less than nine tons of embalmed cats were sold the bones which came from the beni-hassan pit were purchased at 5 17s 6d per ton the heads were separately sold at prices ranging from two to five shillings we suppose a3 curiosities the manure lots being mostly broken in fra foments

results.title: SOME AMERICAN MUMMIES. (Auckland Star, 05 October 1900)
results.fulltext: some american mummies the history of embalming in egypt is well known and it is a more or less interesting study to attempt to compare the making of mummies in the east ana in america with a view to throwing light on the singularities and religious observances which formed a part of the ceremony of mummification from a translation of sepulchural texts in egypt it has been learned that mummies were made there to keep the body inviolate and ready for the return of the soul at the time of resurrection the egyptians seemed to recognise four parts in a man the body the soul an intelligence and an appearance eidolon at death these were separated and then inter-1 vened a period of from three thousand to ten thousand years during this time the soul travelled the under-world as a penance while the intellirnce wandered through space as these parts were to return at the end of the time indicated it was considered necessary to preserve the body from corruption and in the attempts to accomplish this we find the reason for embalming among the ancient egyptians their pyramids their secret burials ana the extraordinary methods of hiding the dead customs which have been of the greatest value to archaeologists and students of man and the human race the embalming process was carried on with greater or less ceremony and expense in proportion to the wealth of the deceased and if the latter were a king or a member of the roya family or a wealthy man no expense was spared to embalm him in a lasting manner and to place the remains in a well built tomb the embalming was carried out on a regular system there being four rituals to grovern it the first related to the incisions to be made in the body the second was a manual treating of the gums resins and spices to be used the bandages and elaborate descriptions as to the method of binding the body and the prayers u be recited at each stage of the work third the water ritual giving the litanies to be recited while the body was being taken by water to its last resting place and fourth the work containing the funeral ritual given when the body was placed in the tomb these books were for the instruction of the priests and operators the drqcess of embalming was divided first came the evisceration taking about two weeks this was followed by the salting or bituminising which took 30 days then came the spicing and bandaging occupying 35 days or 72 days in all the great cemeteries of these days all had establishments fob making mummies attached to them as crematories are found to-day and the professional embalmers constituted an army of people in themselves according to edwards there were never less than 800 bodies in process of mummification in the work-shops of the necropolis of memphis the method of treatment depended upon the rank and wealth of the dead in the case of a poor man the bandages would be coarse but if the deceased was wealthy they were of the finest linen each finder and limb were bound 1250 yards having in some cases been enrolled by investigatorsnearly two tfrirds of a mile of bandages 3in or 4in in width there were many methods of making mummies and time has shown that those of the theban epoch were the best the bodies after centuries being so flexible that they can be bent without breaking this was it is supposed due to the expensive ingredients employed mummies of some kind are found in 1 many lands and it is interesting to note that they occur in-various parts of the united states possibly the most interesting coming from the caves of arizona according to lawson the santee indians of south carolina preserved their dead by embalming with certain roots after which they dried the body and covered it with the bark of the pine or cypress finally the skeleton was secured and wrapped in cloth made of opossum hair the remains being placed in a box others are wrapped in deerskins and stored in the quiogozon which was the royal tomb perfect mummies have been found in the caves of kentucky one enveloped in rough clothes and wrapped in deerskins was found ten feet below the surface in a cave it was the bodyof a woman the hair shaven off according to custom beneath the outer deerskin was another skin of the deer then came a clotn formed of twine inside of this was a cloth resembling this but covered and ornamented with brown feathers the natives of the northt-welit embalmed their dead the body was usually doubled up and placed in a case of fur or grass made for the purpose the alaskan commercial company secured from the seal islands of the company a mummy supposed to be 150 years old which shows that this method of burial has been followed for many years it was discovered on a cave in kagamale island filled with sulphurous vapours which came from crevices in the rock eleven mummies were found one the chief was held by a basket like coffin or structure 4ft in height and evidently made with the greatest care the material with which the remains were wrapped were matting woven from seaweed in a very skilful manner and1 skins amongl which was a fine skin of the sea otter over all was a net made of the sinews of the sea lion in many of the so-called-mummies of america the body was placed in a sitting position several were found by the writer on san clemente island california doubled up the head resting on the knees while in front of the face and behind the head were placed flutes of bone inlaid with the pearly abalone the so-called mummy caves of arizona from which mummies have been taken are very interesting and elaborate1 in their structure one is known as mummy cave ruin and is in del muerto canon and known to the navajos today as tse-i-ya-kih it stands about soft above the bed of the canon on the face of the cliff with a commanding yew and is placed in a natural weathering it is believed that originally there were 20 rooms in the western cave and 14 can be distinguished to-day in the eastern cave about 44 can be distinguished and it is estimated that originally the ruin represented 90 rooms affording a home for possibly 60 people many of the rooms are 20ft wide and 15ft across and were two storeys in height what is called the eastern cave or the mummy cave is to-day a most picturesque ruin and steps have been taken by the government for its preservation the houses of stone are packed in under the great cliff where the stone has weathered out and the failing ruin has aided materially in forming the talus that reaches down covered with the stones used by the ancient builders to the bottom of the canon windows and doors remain intact in many rooms and the storeys can readily be traced by standing walls if these picturesque ruins were in some valley in egypt they would attract the attention of thousands but they are visited by the student and the scientific man alone and by but an occasional tourist who strays into the region in egypt mummies of crocodiles and cats are common but the mummification of animals in america appears to have been rare on the island of san clements mummified dogs have been founa they were tanned in some way and then wrapped in basketry of seaweed

results.fulltext: valuable antiquities not wanted in new zealand the new zealand government i-posaibly not likely to concern itself just now about egyptian and other antiquities but a splendid opportunity topurchase a collection of no fewer than 12905 specimens has been brought under the notice of the director of the dominion museum mr a hamilton mr andre bhcher of cairo whohas spent many years in the collection of those antiquities has written to a now zealand friend asking him to bring under the notice of the government the facb that he is prepared to dispose of the collection for 20000 and the verdict of mr hamilton after going through the catalogue is that the whole would be quite cheapat that price there are nearly five thousand figures vessels weapons and tools in bronze statues stelae reliefs weights amulets vases in alabaster rare boxes for papyrie human mummies also those of crocodiles cats snakes and hawks sarcophagi coffins of papiormache and wood the greco-roman collection of over 5000 pieces is equally comprehensive and complete and in addition there are 80 pieces of jewellery hundreds of beautiful specimens of beads 2soo scarabs engraved gems and a rare number of rare embroideries the only chance of new zealand obtaining sucha magnificent collection of treasures of a period not too well represented in the museums of the do minion is for some rich and patriotic now zealander to come forward with a generous offer a lost opportunity of this kind is brought to mind by the references in the january number of the english scientifio journal nature to a grreat collection of maori antiquities added to the museum of the university of philadelphia by mr e w clark it is much to be regretted remaik-s the journal that this remarkable collection has not found a home in one of our imperial or colonial museums

granite table i had remained unconscious throughout seventy days for such i know was the length of time a mummy is left to soak in nitre i was embalmed thethmosis and his assistants wrapped me carefully in long bands of flax coated with gum and soon i was completely shrouded in several thicknesses of linen cloth a strang thing happened and one which was a serious departure from the usual results.title: INTO THE LAND OF EGYPT—16 Where Crocodiles were Gods (Ellesmere Guardian, 11 October 1938)
results.fulltext: into the land of egypt16 where crocodiles were gods t wanted to be moving i wanted to get away from cairo where europeans and egyptians are so kind and so hospitable that you continue to stay on there long after you should have left like dublin cairo is a difficult city to leave because people are so friendly invite you out write letters to you ring you up on the telephone and offer to take you here there and everywhere it requires great strength of mind to leave cairo it would indeed be easy to come to egypt and see nothing except that city however one night when i was reading in bed in the shadow of the pyramids i decided to hire a car tlfe next morning and go to the fayum i thought the fayum would be interesting because i had been reading strabo and herodotus for in the old daysthe first four centuries before christgreek and roman tourists always went to the fayum to see the sacred crocodiles at arsinoe i suppose some pre christian thomas cook advertised them as a sight which no visitor to egypt should miss the crocodiles were kept in a sacred lake in the grounds of the temple of sebek they wore gold earrings and splashed the water with forepaws decorated with jewelled bracelets the visitor was expected to make offerings of fried fish and honey cakes but it is clear from the accounts of ancient writers that the crocodiles would have preferred the visitor himself the priests had a trick of opening the crocodiles mouths without getting hurt stealing up as the animals were asleep in the sun they quickly opened their mouths and injected the fried fish and honey cakes leaping back as the crocodiles jumped angrily into the water it is surprising that none of those cynical greeks ever wrote a dialogue between a sacred crocodile and a sacred cow on the horror of being a god to-day the sacred ponds are dried up and there are vast dusty mounds where the temple stood sometimes natives digging in the earth find the mummy of a crocodile brittle as old wood wrapped in yards of fine linen early in the morning i set out for the fayum the road leaves the pyramids to plunge for forty miles across a blinding desert forty miles of desert are just enough to show you what a desert is like but not enough to fill your heart with despair and weariness the sandy track loses itself on a featureless horizon the sand hills shoulder each other mile after mile here smooth as brown velvet there rippled with the wind as if the tide had just gone out and the sun beats angrily upon this dead land until the eyes grow weary and sore with looking at the burning flatness until any objecta bird the white bones of a camel the chassis of a burnt-out ford car comes as a welcome relief from the monotonous sterility one feature of the desert is beauti by h v morton ful the dry clean air it is like the air on top of ben nevis and when you have lived in an eastern city for some time where the air is full of all sorts of things the desert air blowing over thousands of miles of clean sand stirs up the bloodstream and cheers the heart still what a joy it is to see far off the first glimpse of palm trees and to know that in a short time you will enter the first patch of shade hear the gurgle of running water and listen with delight to the sound of birds the fayum is an oasis lying about 140 feet below the level of the mediterranean the arabs say that it was made fertile by the vizier yusuf who caused canals to be dug which brought water and life to the desert the vizier yusuf is the joseph of the bible the track led downhill towards a scene that looked to me like a child impression of the garden of eden the desert ended suddenly against a wall of date palms high up where the fronds spray upwards against the blue sky i saw bunches of date lying like a swarm of bees in heavy clusters the colour of spanish mahogany instead of the barren sand the road now lay along a high embankment of black earth the rich pregnant black earth of egypt and on either side ran slow canals of fresh waterthe veins that carry the life blood of this land the richness of the fayum was proverbial in the days of the pharaohs it was a land with the climate of paradise and to-day it is farmed by the rich landowners of egypt some of whom even know their own farms by sight and attend to the details lof farm management the earth produces almost anything that is sown in it oranges bananas mandarins dates sugar-cane rice maize and the only real crop of olives grown in egypt i the strangest of all the fayum products are sea fish how can sea fish come from an oasis in the desert 150 miles from the sea the answer is that the water of lake karoun a salt lake on the western boundary is chemically much the same as the mediterranean sea how hard the fellah works with what unremitting toil must he slave at this black land giving his life in return for its fruitfulness every head of maize is literally won at the cost of his sweat and the cracking of his muscles he stands to the waist in water his single thin garment drenched with the drip of the shaduf he stands in the clinging mud of the fields the soles of his bare feet making him an easy victim to the terrible germ that lives in the soil of egypt he stands bowed above his virginian plough he strides like pharaoh soldiers on a temple wall slashing at the man-high maize stalks he staggers covered like a jack-in-the green burdened with a load of bersim every day year in and year out century after century it is the same he is the fellah the man whose sweat built the pyramids and the temples the man whose indomitable sense of fatality is perhaps the most colossal of egypt monuments as i pass his pretty villages built in groves of date palms beside shallow canals i smell the wood smoke rising from the ovens where his women are baking the tough bread which is his staple food i see the little mud houses where he goes home to sleep for a few hours before the sun like a trumpet in the morning calls him out to strive again with water and with mud and there is little inside his house of four walls of mud except little children playing in the dust but the fellah is asleep in the wide and comfortable arms of ignorance over 85 per cent of the population of egypt is unable to read and who looking around at the fruits of so-called knowledge to-day would wish to awaken the fellah from his ancient slumber i travelled through the villages to the edge of lake karoun where a small two-storey hotel kept by a young german stands within a few yards of the water edge the hotel was empty because it was mid-week at the week-ends it is filled with sportsmen from cairo who come to shoot the countless thousands of wild duck snipe and teal which haunt the lake-side and i thought that this lake was the most beautiful thing i had seen so far in egypt it is a sheet of blue water lying in the sunlight with the tawny desert on its western shores a desert in which lie forgotten cities of the greek age and old temples falling into dust a few poor fishermen row about the lake with their nets and sell their catches on the shore in the still hush of this remote place the blend of blue water and desert hills i was reminded of another lakethe lake of galilee an arab servant took my bag up to a little bedroom overlooking the lake the bed was covered with a mosquito net and the room smelt cleanly of camphor i have just opened the hotel said young mr schumacher the proprietor for i keep it shut until the shooting season opens what a business it is opening a hotel that has been shut for an egyptian summer the lizards the snakes the birds and the frogs come and live here also the wild bees i knew that i was going to like karoun

results.title: AT THE GATES OF THE DESERT. (Bush Advocate, 29 April 1909)
results.fulltext: at the gates of the desert by a banker guarding the approach to that arid and barren ocean of driven sand tho libyan desert and almost beneath the shadow of the mightiest structure ever stretched by man nion this earth stands that strange wonder of the ancient world the gret sphinx and well might those superstitious and deluded worshippers of crocodiles and mummied cats of osiris and horns and ptah regard the impassive monster with awe and with the ptofoundcst reverence well might they look upon it as endowed with tremendous authority and power and with the absolute control over their destinies both in this life and in the realms beyond the tomb for to us even of this more intelligent age emancipated from those insensate delusions which held those mighty ancients in an iron grip and sunk them down in abysmal and benighted ignorance it is a thrilling experience to stand at sunset before the towering majestic form of the stupendous figure now starting as it were into life as the golden rays merge into oarinine and the passionless visage is gradually mantled with af suffused ever deepening blush as though the life-blood were coursing through itj now as the great red luminary sinks lower and lower the roseate hue of vitality fading away into a sullen and lurid empurpled lividity and now as the gloaming advances and the stars of heaven one by one shine forth the massive features of the image darkening ever blacker and deeper until the rising moon again rekindles on it a ghostly aud unearthly pallor hoary with age a thousand years before menephtah generals vainly pursuing the israelite host perished ignpminiously in tire lied sea the blear stony eyes of this sculptured monster of the past a huge and stupendously colossal man-headed lion itspedastal a rock-hewn temple have looked out with the same impenetrable visionless gaze upon some of the greatest events of this world history the triumphant progresses of the great rameses the headlong flight of pharoah necho driven back by the invincible forces of nebuchadnezzar the return of shishak with his rich plunder from the holy city jerusalem or the victorious triumph of that mighty rider of a worldempire alexander the great and then later on after many another stirring vicissitude three weary figiu-es fleeing by divine command from the murderous jealousy of herod who wotild not suffer his kingly power to be disputed by another even though a babe the reputed father the mother and tho holy child take refuge in egypt doubtless regarding tlie stupendous fane with equal wonder as we ourselves at this day but that helpless child was the lord of glory who in order to save mankind from the consequences of his sins left his throne in tho heaven of heavens for a time and himself satisfied the claims of eternal justice by bearing the punishment due and whosoever will may participate in tlxat allprftvaihiig quittance

results.fulltext: recent discoveries in egypt an interesting collection of antiquities has lately been on exhibition in london consisting of the various objects brought to light by mr flinders petrie during his recent excavations in egypt at hawera on the sie of the ancient labrinth described by herodotns these objects are not so very ancient that is they belong to the ptolemaic arid roman periods which although dating back to about 300 8c is quite modern according to the egyptian standard nevertheless to many people these relics which speak so eloquently of the manners and customs of the romans in egypt from about the birth of christ to 200 ad and of the preceding ptolemies better known to us historically than their ancient predecessors the pharaohs will be of more interest than those of far greater antiquity the first thing which strikes us is a series of portraits on wood so perfect and fresh in appearance that it is difficult to believe that they have been buried for nearly 2000 years yet such is the case for these portraits represent romans interred during the ptolemaic period it is singular that the romans in egypt should have adopted the mode of burial of the egyptians but the faces and dress of these portraits are undoubtedly roman although they cohered the heads of mummies beautifully and elegantly swathed in the numerous linen bandages peculiar to egyptian burials but more artistically arranged than was common in the more ancient mummies for the crossings of the bandages form j a beautiful honeycomb pattern of extraordi j jaary symmetry each panel finished with a gilt band the board upon which the por i trait was painted was bandaged in skilfully j over the head and thus the relatives might have the mournful pleasure of contemplating the features of the deceased whenever j fchey pleased and certainly no artist even of modern times eoqld have more faithfully pourtrayed the individual than did the portrait painter of 2000 years ago they are evidently what are usually called speaking likeaesses there is one of an old man who might have been a general or one of the csesars in fete white toga avery line and furrow of the face carefully delineated whilst several of the iad3 and particularly j two young girls might he exhf bed as like nesses of professional beauties of the present day the material employed for these dur able portraits was a wax medium which has been employed with excellent effeot in modern times and might be used more fre quently with advantaga the beautiful views of greece in the neve pinakothek at munich executed by order of the old king ludwig are of this kind and we believe some of the pictures in the houses of parliament westminster are also painted on wax the mummies wifch the portraits were generally deposited in unadorned wooden coffins with movable lids these coffins which are not made of slabs of wood but of small pieces neatly joined are raised a few inches from the ground upon four short feet and beside them were placed the tour canopic vases with animal heads containing the viscera such as are always found in egyptian tombs several of these jars are exhibited by mr petrie as well as some of the flint knives used ceremonially long after the invention of iron by the embalmers in making the necessary incisions in the body there are also to be seen funeral wreaths one still adorning the head of a mummy made of flowers the species of which are still distinguishable wheat barley and other seeds grasses and leaves of shrubs still more curious are a number of toys some of which are almost identical with those j prized by boys and girls of to-day there are spinning-tops for the boys jointed dolls for the girls and a rag-doll for baby a vooden bird on wheels and other animals including a crocodile a toy bedsteaf and a sedan-chair in terra-eotta containing a lady who can be moved at pleasure i the domestic arts ale by fragments of beautiful embroideries a set of bobbins such as are sifll used for lace-making a bundle of lelther workers needles and awl spindles am a dress made of coarse linen with two brtad purple bands inserted just as repre seited in some of the portrlto the purple balds probably denoting the rank of the worer there is also a pair of short knitted soismade to tie round the ukle aud with a slparate division for the great toe this of course was for the convenience of the werer of sandals but it is amusing to find that the fad of the hygiehisfcs of the heith i exhibition is at least as ancient as thephristian era only the egyptians hud a reaf in for separated toes which thoso who wea boots have not perhaps one of the most interesting of the c-bjets discovered is a lens of thick glass resenbling the bulls-eye of a lanlern but suggesting the possibility that the egyptlantmight have known more of the magnifyinj power of glass than we give them ere for and may even have possessed telejopes aarge case at one end of the room in the bgyfcian hallin which mr flinders petrie cliscveries are appropriately exhibited con a ijautiful collection of egyptian antiquities of anolder date than those we have been de hpribig hundreds of thoso well-known curias little images of gods in blue porflelain jewels of gold necklaces rings braoelets hd ear-rings among which we noticed spmeine pearls numerous scarabgei and other curious and interesting objects serving to show the high development of art in egypt at a very early period where shall we lopk for the beginning of that art 1 in mr flinders petrie collection we see it as it existed in roman times in the british museum we can trace it back into far remote pre-hiatoric times but it seems even then as vigorous and in many 1 respects as perfect as in the more modern period yet buried beneath the magnificent ruins of the cities and tombs of the pharaohs and even incorporated with the tufa out of which these tombs were constructed are found rude flint implements telling of a time when all this magnificent civilisation had no existence where shall we look for the transition stage the period between the users of flint implements and the builders of the pyramids and how shall we estimate the time which has elapsed since the valley of the nile was first occupied by man the recent discoveries of mr flinders petrie and fellow-workers have done much to elucidate doubtful points in egyptian history we are daily discovering proofs of the truthfulness of the writings of herodotus lake mceris and the labyrinth are no longer myths the shepherd kings have been made known to us and the pharaohs of joseph 1 and of moses seem to be identified who shall say how much more of the 1 hidden story written on the stones and on the tombs of ancient egypt may be revealed to us by the zealous explorers of whom mr flinders petrie is chief let us hope that the british museum may be enriched by these recent finds chambers journal

results.title: GERMANY DAY BY DAY. (Clutha Leader 18-5-1915)
results.fulltext: GERMANY DAY BY DAY. Someone has been brightening up Berlin with an extraordinary practical joke. A few dare ago, according to the, 'Berliner Tageblatt,' a largo number of ladies and gentlemen in Berlin 'received by post printed invitations to attend a "re-covering of ancient mummies in the Old' Museum." The cards were in this form: Invitation for February 28. —Old Museum. Re-rolling of Ancient Mummies. For the Directors. P.S.—The orders of the attendants must be obeyed. Several hundred well-dressed Berlinore duly appeared at the Old Museum on the 28th and awaited admission. But the museum was closed. At last some genius was struck with an idea. Of course, the Berlin mummies are all in the New Museum, and the cards must have been misprinted. So off the whole company tramped to the New Museum. This was open, but when the janitor saw the first invitation card he shook his head and' grinned. He fetched a whole hierarchy of officials, and finally the director himself came to explain that Berlin had once more been hoaxed. « * * * * The premium 011 marriageable men in Germany is illustrated by this impudent advertisement in the Munich 'Neueste Nachrichten': Wanted, a noble, artistic. Christian young lady to provide young academician with opportunity to study music; marriage included; lady's fortune intended to provide untroubled existence. Paper coals are the latest substitute recommended I'or use by the poorer classes of the Berlin population. The method) of manufacture, according to the 'Vowsiselle,' is a.s follows: Aowspapers are soaked in water for ISG hours, then they M'e rolled tightly into a bail and left to dry. They 'become as h?>d and l firm as a piece of wood. These paper coals do not burn, but they attain a red glow like real coals, and produce, a considerable degree of heai. especially if used in closed iioves in conjunction with briquets. These paper coals and: one briquet (coal-dust mixed with tar and pressed into an oblong form) suffice for boiling one pound of meat. The official 'North German Gazette' issues an appeal to employers of domestic servants to persuade tneni to invest their savings in the German war loan. ''This is not merely your duty to the State," says this quaint appeal, "it is also your duty to the servant. For why should your poor servant girl be content with the 3 or 31 per cent, of the savings banks when she can invest her savings with the greatest pos- • siljle security in the war loan and get 5 per cent, for 10 years?" Empoyers are not to imagine that l; our Anna's savings" will make no ; difference. "You sho.ild rather con- j sider how many Annas there are in the ' German Empire with .to, or even sev- j eral times £3, saved up. All these l'~/ i together make many millions of ! marks." Having robbed the children's money-boxes the great and wealthy j Germany now purposes to steal the ] housemaids' savings. But the German ; Anna is no fool. There are several . hundreds of thousands of her now work- I iug lor board and lodging without ; wages, and she will keep her savings where they are handy. I The German police arc "downy birds." They liavc foiliid that the surest way of discovering any foreigner who happens to be residing in Germany without being notified to the police is to prevent his getting any bread until he reports himself. Over 100 foreigners were thus discovered in Berlin, and, owiiif} to the usefulness of the bread l ticket control to the police, the Government has refused all requests Irom Cologne- and other cities to relieve them of the expense of introducing the tickets which arc economically unnecessary. A vigorous description o| lh« client of French artillery lire is gvicn m the 'Cologne Gazette' by a German officer lighting in the Champagne. "I believe it to be impossible to describe a French artillery assault, and to be subjected to it for hours is for me the most appalling experience ol the war. . . Our trenches and wire entanglements have looked as if they had been turned by a giant plough. Our whole camp was so shot to pieces that vou could no longer see a sign of the shelters or anything else. After the firing one's nerves are as if dead. Recently we have t:iken to driving galleries from 12ft to loft deep in the trenches, but even this docs not always help." Jenny, the elephant sent to the frontby Hagetibeck, has been given some companions to make her quarters seem more homelike. Prolessor Wegener, the correspondent of the 'Cologne Gazette,' says that her keeper found some animals from a deserted menagerie and put them with the elephant. She has now two cages of apes and ueacocks in her stable. Originally there was a crocodile, but this died. The Hamburg-American Line, like the North German Lloyd, has announced that it will present no balance-sheet this year. For good reasons. "Women, according to the 'Hamburger "Nachrichten,' are to be employed as platform porters for shutting doors, etc., on local electric railways in Germany. The men hitherto employed are required for service in Belgium. Germans have discovered a very good omen. Count Zeppelin has at last a grandson to carry on the name. His only child, Hella, who married a von Brandenstein and was granted the name Brandeiistein-Zeppelin, has a son. Baron von Ivuenssberg, director of the One-Armed War Cripples' School at Heidelberg, begs the public to desist from gazing at every one-armed man who now appears in the street as if he were a rare show, a beggar, or a barrel organist. "When you see a one-armed man in the street in uniform yon should see in the empty sleeve a' mark of honor for the man and for yourself a warning to take *his Holy War very seriously."

results.fulltext: the treasures of egypt greek scholars of the present gener i atioii have enjoyed and are stillenjoying a unique experience writes mr f g kenyon in an extremely able and informed article in the quarterlyreview the uniqueness of theirexperience lies in the fact that to them alone i has it been vouchsafed to recover from the sands of egypt a rapid succession of greek works which no human eye had seen for perhaps a millennium and a-half the year 1891 may be indeed be said without the exaggeration which usually attends the phrase to have been epoch-making for it marked the beginning of a new period the importance of which in the history of greek literature cannot be denied in that year professor mahaffy published the first part of the petrie papyri so-called after their discoverer professor flinders petrie which included portions of the p4lo of plato and the lost antiope of euripides together with smaller fragments of homer and other authorswritten upon papyrus in the early part of the third century 8c 600 years earlier than the earliest biblical mss then known and 1300 years earlier than the generality of greek classical mss at the beginning of 1904 it was calculated that the number of published literary papyri large and 6mall wasapproximately 350 without reckoning theological texts which might have been estimated at another 60 of these about 160 contained texts not previously known about 110 conl tamed portions of homer and the remaining 80 were divided among other already extant works the leading places being taken by demosthenes and plato since then very considerable additions have been made to these figures so that the totalof published literary papyri now falls little short of 600 and so far from being exhausted is the supply that the year 1907 in its concluding month established its claim to rank with 1897 with 1891 and with 1847 as one of the anni mirabiles in the fortunes of greek literature so much for the past what of the future the answer is simple the experience of the last few months has shown us that the treasures of egypt are not exhausted if a casualscratchingin a paltry village can give us back menander and a search for an ancient egyptian interment can as a by-prodtictj reveal a greek soldier buried with a roll of timotheus why should not similar chances give u6 sappho simohides stesichoruß archilochus cratinus agsthon and others for whom out mouths water or like herodas almost unknown writers of unsuspected interest we know that the works of most or all of these were in existence during the period covered by tho papyri and for the rest we depend upon fortune there are still many rubbish-heaps left in egypt and it is from themthe mounds which surround the sites of ancient towns and villagesthat most of the papyri though not the most perfect have come there must still be cemeteries containing mummy-eae-s made out of masses of papyrus compacted together and covered wiih clny biro that of gurob and hibeb there may still be mummified crocodiles to bo found stuffed and wrapped round with papyrus rolls like those of tebtuim there may still occasionally bo found pofi containing manuscripts like those which produced the mcuander or the papyri from the serapeum of thebes or burials in which a manuscript has boon laid with the dead man like the timotboiis at abusir or the hyperrides ms obtained by bankes nnd arden near thebes but these things lie upon the knees of tho gods it is for scholars at home to support and facilitate the work of those who go out to search and to prepare themselves and their posterity to deal with tlie accessions which they bring to that immortal greek literatureupon which our civilisation ibaed

results.fulltext: sport or slaughter the saturday review thus comments on the above under the heading of sport or slaughter the feeling avith which we lay before our readers this chronicle of lord londesborough doings in egypt is by no means akin to the pleasure entertained by the field disgust and indignation is rather the sentiment which we entertain and which aye believe will also be felt by the sportsmen avho are readers of our contemporarydisgust and indignation not only as regards the flunkeyism which chronicles the cost of the equipment which is so expensive and which is only within the reach of wealthy men like the noble lordbut disgust and indignation at the scandalous poulterer bill which the noble lord or his valet has sent to the fiell lord londesborough is the son of one who wa3 known as an art collector of some taste and aye wishthat the son had followed in his father path possibly he is an accomplished archaeologist he may be skilled like moses in all the learning of egypt and he may be bringing home sculptures mummies and papyri he may be about to enrich the department of antiquities at the british museum but he certainly avill do nothing to illustrate its ornithology if he has only gone to the nile as a variety to the excitement of a battue we can but regret in the interests alike of humanity decency and science that he did riot confine himself to the common-place butchery of a norfolk pheasant-shooting there is no sport avhatever in slaughtering the poor harmless birds of the upper nile while there is something inexpressibly ludicrous and humiliating in the fact that a great english lordat vast expense is at the trouble of being towed along that sacred river and through the heart of that mighty land of mystery and ancient civil izition for the dignified purpose of furnishing the readers ot the field avith the importantfact that it took his lordship two months to murder 1514 of those geese which a fellow-feeling might have prompted him to spare to ruu up 500 miles of the nile for the high and sacred object of popping successfully at 3283 pigeons avhich might have shown as good sport at hornsey wood is a feat which reflects small credit on the british nobility lord londesborough has done something positively detrimental to science and to society besides a brutal and avholesate butchery of wild game he has done wrong to the world beyond egypt 112 herons and storks we trust is a mistake on the nile the poor herons utterly useless for food share the fish of that abounding stream with the crocodiles and as to the storks they are the pride and delight of the people living on the banks of that classic river they build on the house-tops walk tame and fearless through the alluvial fields destroy noxious vermin and are regarded by the peasants in the same familiar and domestic aspect as the british robin among ourselves besides all this they are the very birds whia spend the summer in holland and spain and if in the cities of europe we miss our sacred and migratory storks we shall have to thank the j british sportsman on the nile shoull it ever become a fool passion among idle young men to follow lord londesborough example as to j the forty-seven flamingoes words are too faint jto express the outrage upon every feeling avhich is caussed by the shameless and wanton massacre of a bird of singular grace and beauty and to which the nile scenery owes so much and which even in upper egypt is by no means common

results.fulltext:
GERMANY DAY BY DAY. Someone luns been brightening up Berlin with an extraordinary practical joke. A few (toys igo, according to the 'Berliner TiageblaU,' a krgo number of ladies and gentlemen in Berlin awotv«d by post printed invitations to attend a "re-covering of Ancient mummies i" the Oldi Museum.' The cards were in this fawn: Invitation for February 2-B.—Old Museum. Re-rolling of Ancient Mummies. For the Directors. P.S.—The orders of tho attendants must by obeyed. Several hundred well-dressed Berlinel's duly appeared at the Old Museum on the'2Bth and awaited l admission. But the museum was closed. At last some genius was struck with tin idea. Of course, the Berlin nmmimies are all in the New Museum, and the cards must Jiave been misprinted. So off tho wholo company tramped to the New Museum. This was open, but when the janitor saw tho first invitation c«ird ho shook his head and grinned. Ho fetched a whole hierarchy of officials, and 1 finally the director himself came to explain that Berlin had once more been hoaxed. The premium on marriageable men in . Germany is illustrated by this impudent advertisement in the Munich 'Neuesto Nachriehtcn': Wanted, a noble, .artistic, Christ ton young fiidy to provide young academician with opportunity to study music; marriage included; lady's fortune intended to provide untroubled existence. Paper coals aro the latest substitute, I recommended for use by the poorer classes of the Berlin population. The method of manufacture, according to the 'Vowische,' is as follows: Newspapers are soaked in water for 36 hours, then they are rolled tightly into a bad and left to dry. They become as haul and firm as a. piece, of wood. These paper coals do not burn, but they attain a, red glow like real coals, and produce a considerable degree of heat, especially if used in closed doves in conjunction with briquets. These paper coals and one briquet (oosil-dnst mixed willi far and 1 pressed into an oblong form) suffice for boiling one pound of meat. The official 'North German Gazette' issues an appeal Io employers of domestic servants to persuade tuem to invest their savings in the German war loan. ''This is not merely your duty to the State," says this quaint appeal, ''it is also your duty to the servant. for why should your poor servant girl be i-onien! with the ', or 3J per cent, of the savings banks when she can invest her saving with the greatest possible security il. the war loan and get 5 per (.'lit. for i ) years:-''' JCnipi vers are not to i'uagine that "our .
na's s.icings" CII make no difference. ''You should rather consider how many An nils there are in the German Umpire with Co, or even *eve ai times Co, saved tip. All these Co together make many millions of naiks." ilaving robbed the children's iie.iney-boM's the great ind. wealthy Germany now pin pases to steal the housemaids' savings. Uiii. the German Anna is no fool. There are several hundreds of thousands of her now working tor board and lodging without wages, and she will keep her savings where tliev are handy. The German police are "downy birds.' They have round that the surest' way of discovering any foreigner who happens to be residing in Germany without being notified to the police is to prevent his geftini; any bread until he reports himself. Over 100 foreigner:, were thus disoou'red in Berlin, and, owing to tin; usefulness „f the breadticket control to the poliee, the-Governinriit has reliised all requests horn Cdog .. ami (the- citi"-. to relieve them of the "xpinse of introducing the ti.'kets which are economically unnecessary. A vigorous description of tlio ellect of French artillery fire is gvion in the 'Cologne Gazette' by a German officer lighting in the Champagne. -'I heliuve it to be impossible lo describe a French artillery assault, and to be subjected to it for hours is lor me the most appalling experience of the war. . . , Our trenches and wire entanglements have looked as if they had been turned by a giant plough. Our whole camp was to shot to pieces that you could no longer see a sign of the .shelters or anything else. After the firing one's nerves are as if dead. Recently we have taken to driving galleries from 12ft to 15ft deep in the trenches, but even this does not always help." Jenny, the elephant sent to the front by Hagenbeck, has been given some companions jo make her quarters seem more homelike. Professor Wegener, the correspondent of the 'Cologne Gazette,' says that her keeper found eomo animals from a deserted menagerio and put them with tlio elephant. She has now two cages of apes and neacocks in her stable. Originally there was a crocodile, but this died. The Hamburg-American Line, like the North German Lloyd, has announced that it will present no balance-sheet this year. For good reasons. Women, according to the 'Hamburg-, er Nachrichten,' are to be employed' as platform porters for shutting doors, : etc., on local electric railways in Ger- ! many. The men hitherto employed are required for service in Belgium. Germans have discovered a very good omen. Count Zeppelin has at last a grandson to carry on the name. His only child, Hella, who married a von Brandenstein and was granted the name ISrandenstein-Zeppelin, has a son. Baron von Kuenssberg, director of the One-Armed War Cripples' Sclwol at Heidelberg, begs the public to desist from gazing at every one-armed man who now appears in the street as if lie were a rare show, a beggar, or a barrel organist. "When you seo a one-armed man in the street in uniform you should see in the empty sleeve a marl, of honor for the. man and for yourself a warning to take *his Holy War very seriously."

results.title: EDISON'S GREAT JOKE. (Otago Witness, 28 May 1891)
results.fulltext: edison great joke the most astounding feabt in the i hibtoey of stbangb repasts mr edison is a strange man ani his practical jokes are not the least curious of his many scientific prank 3 his latest humorous essay was an electric dinner party given in honour of the members of the club which is composed of admirers of the great benjamin franklin the dinner was held at edison factory and the chair was taken by a life-size wax model of franklin dressed just as he looked 150 years ago it was a figure that moved and spoke a phonograph was concealed in the interior of the model and ben franklin every now and then gave forth one of his famous moral axioms the laboratory had teen transformed from its workaday world appearance as if by magic in the centre o the room there was a long narrow table the ordinary work-bench of the place covered with snow-white napery and adorned with what looked like luscious fruits fresh flowers and sparkling glass some of the fruit and flowers were real enough twas certain but what was true and what was anificial it would have taken solomon to ascertain the guests sat down and were served with the first course there was no chef employed it was cooked by electricity and in face so was everything i down to the coffee which was made over wires the diners had no sooner got their teeth into samples from a deliciously stewed dish of oysters when bang 1 out went the incandescent lights and darkness reigned ihen there appeared out of the shadows a coupli of hideoug grinning skulls their eyes shone fire their mouths shot forth flame 3 their jaws moved with a snapping like a crocodiles and from their invisible throats there came forth two sepulchral voice 3in ucison aa ye are now bo once were we as we are now ao re shall be it was a pleasing appetiser mr edison had as if by magic brought them out of space somehow and bad by tbe subtle use of a battery and a phonograph made eyes gleam were in reality only sockets were and their fleshless jaws move as if alive mr edison has a friend who has a deep bass voice which seems to issue from his feet and he it was who was pressed into service for the manufacture of the phonographic sound--of course after the mechanism of the thing was explained every man had a good laugh at his neighbour but the apparition of the grinning speaking skulls one of which in life bad been detached from its body be the gullotine was ghastly in the extreme it was a sort of reminiscence of the old egyptian mummy at the feast the lights were turned up again and another course was introduced all unsuspecting the various guests began to enjoy the viands cooked by electricity but with ben franklin at the table there was small chance for sybaritic enjoyment of the meal he sat smiling an oily benignant smile when suddenly there issued from his waxen gullet the following sententious maxim a fat kitchen makes a lean will if you would know the value of money try and borrow some and all the time the old philosopher sat there smiling unperturbed it was a mean trick for the frugal old philosopher of colonial days to play on the degenerate pleasure-loving scion of the present time and so the dinner went on in the midst of it suddenly there burst forth from the phonograph the sovnd of a delicious voioe it was madame adinis of the grand opera in paris she sang a few notes and then suddenly there merged into hers the deep notes of a rich basso that was melchissedecs together they were pouring forth the inspiring music of the marsellaise next there came the booming of cannon the thrilling notes of a grand bugle solo with its echoes against the buildings of paris and finally a man voice again making a graceful little address you could hear the plaudits of a crowd the all hail of a populace which was crying out as with one voice vive la france i vive la republique i vive carnot 1 by the dexterous placing of a phonograph the guests at the strange little dinner in america had been transported across the atlantic and were listening to the last closing exercises of the paris exhibition of 1889 the man voice distinctly heard making a speech was m eiffels in the place that a centrepiece would naturally occupy in the ordinary dinner the lights suddenly went out again and a stbange thing happened near the middle of the table there had been throughout the dinner a great globe of gold-fishes through which flashed the variedcoloured lights that had been turned on from time to time all of a sudden as if a magi i cian had waved his wand the globe became illumined with a monochrome in the globe of glass were seen swimming about the little live fishes of gold or silver which were illumined internally by electricity all the anatomy of the shiny fishes was plainly discernible and they swam and swam about as if nothing more unusual had occurred than was natural with the finny folk yet each one of these fishes had inserted down his throat down into his stomach a miniature elecric light about the size of a big pea and was sailing about with a thin hair-like wire in its gullet that was almost invisible to the naked eye this of course was attached to a dynamo which produced the light that transfigured their little bodies and the effect that the display produoed was wonderful so the dinner went on and with every course with every other minute some strange uncanny thing was done by the magical intervention of electricity the oysters were stewed by the same mystical force so were the eggs boiled so the water for the punch was heated and then just as the guests were swallowing the last but one oyster on their plates or smacking their lips after the draining of a glass of electric punch something odd and cbeepy took place between whiles once for instance the lights went out and there appeared on the tablea miniature menagerie the inmates of which had blazing eyep mouths spitting forth flames like the animals in the apocalypse and all were doing some surprising thing everyone as he sat down had noticed the stuffed bear the crocodile the longnecked heron and other specimens of the kind which adorned the table but everyone looked upon them as mere ornaments and nothing else yet in the twinkling of an eye the bear became blue the heron green the crocodile pink and during the illumination a visitor present swore that he saw the crocodile shed tears but nothing was remarkable at this banquet and all the time benjamia franklin was sitting quietly before the cloth not saying muoh after he had delivered his speech of welcome once in a while some sententious bit of wisdom like indus ry pays debts while despair increaseth them dropped sepulchrally from his lips he had not made his presence felt for some time when towards the end of the dinner darkness prevailed once more and a flash of lightning ilutninated iho room ben franklin had agdin called down the lightning from the skies over in a corner of the place there had boen fixed a kiie which everyone had supposed was a part of the decorations but it had a special purpose and when the room was darkened this time this weird waxen image by some incantation of mr edison repeated the experiment famous to every schoolboy by which electricity was first discovered cigarettes were lighted by electricity after that the coffee was brewed on the table by electricity and the cgars and cigarettes were passed from one guest to another along a miniature toy railway that ran on a track about the table the latter could only 00 lighted by electricity as no matches provided during the dinner it was no uncommon thing for a man to pick up a plate and drop it again as if it were a bomb it had been charged heavily with the same force and was one of the many quiet jokes that were perpetrated during the evening just as the banquet was ending all the flowers overhanging the table fell in showers i upon the guests below tiny bits of iron j had been attached to each rose and carnation which were held in their places by the attraction of the magnet when the circuit was broken the flowery shower followed tbe air was kept cool all the time by steel fans worked by electricity and among the numerous other odd things that happened was the sudden burst of piano music that broke in upon the banquet this was produced by a subtle telephonic connection with a piano in the next street played by a young woman who was notified by a local telegraph when her services were required mr edison through the medium of a phonographic cylinder made some pleasant remarks about franklin and through a like medium de wolf hopper robust voice filled the apartment with the topical song you can always explain it away 1 at 11 oclock sharp the strident voice of franklin quietly remarked marly to bed and early to rlie makes a man healthy wealthy and wlie and so the strange dinner was over

results.title: INTO THE LAND OF EGYPT—9 The Zoo on the Nile (Ellesmere Guardian, 13 September 1938)
results.fulltext: into the land of egypt9 the zoo on the nile by h v morton itttere it possible to bring to life the mummy of an ancient egyptian one of the things that would surprise him would be the disappearance of wild animals from his native land centuries ago as the pictures on the tombs and sculptures in the temples prove egypt was a country in which the hippopotamus the crocodile and the lion were frequently hunted i to-day these animals have deserted egypt although they are still found far to the south in the sudan i this is probably because a greater area of land is now under cultivation and in the fact that the nile in flood no longer creates new marshes every year in which wild animals can make their lairs most of the animals in egypt to-day are domesticated the donkey the camel the buffalo the horse the goat the sheep the dog and the cat they are seen everywhere in great numbers and they live in close companionship with their owners the egyptian peasant is a gentle kindhearted easy-going soul until his latent fanatacism is roused and i would not call him consciously cruel to animals in fact one sees a starving dog with his ribs bursting through his hide less frequently in egypt than in any other moslem country the cat which in egypt kills snakes as well as rats and mice occupies a curiously privileged position no egyptian would dream of killing a cat he might refuse to pull a drowning cat out of water but he would never throw it in in the atmosphere of almost superstitious awe which surrounds the cat i am sure we can see a j relic of the cat worship of ancient egypt more unpleasant creatures such as snakes and bats and insects of every kind abound in the dry hot air of egypt the deadly cobra which in ancient times was the symbol of royalty is still found all over the nile valley in town and country although it is frequently killedl have seen a policeman shoot one with his revolverl have heard that in certain villages a cobra that takes up its abode in the cellar of a mud house is sometimes venerated as the guardian of the hearth and is fed on eggs and chickens i have been unable to verify this one or two people who know egypt well have laughed at the story but the person who told it to me knows egypt equally well and is a reliable observer i do know however that the peasant attributes extraordinary in i telligence fa the cobra a country police officer whom i met outside cairo told me a story which i do not believebut i am sure he did which illustrates this fellah attitude to this snake he said that in a village in upper egypt where he was once stationed two cobras hatched a family of young snakes in the cellar of a mud house one day the children of the house discovered the little cobras lying in the sun and began to tease them with sticks the female cobra appeared and coiled herself round the body of the smallest child and the cries of the infant brought out the man and his wife the parents were terrified but to have made one move against the cobra would have caused the death of the child suddenly the woman cried out perhaps if our children stop tormenting her children she will go away the father ran over to his children and gave them a sound thrashing whereupon the cobra quietly uncurled herself and went away i have no idea whether you can believe this even if it is not true it shows that the fellah attributes human understanding to the cobra and other stories which are told up and down the nile invest the horrible reptile with mysterious qualities the same police officer swore that he knew a certain village in which a cobra was in the habit of visiting a certain woman but only when her husband was away he said that he would never have believed this had he not seen the cobra coiled up peacefully near her neck such stories surely suggest that reverence for the royal snake has come down to the modern egyptians from ancient times every other kind of snake is killed on sight notably the horned viper the most deadly snake in egypt whose bite can cause death in twenty minutes but i must return to the subject of this article which is the cairo zoo having nothing particular to do one morning i decided to go there although i dont usually like the sight of animals in cages a taxi took me in about fifteen minutes to a beautiful garden on the west bank of the nile it is entered j through a charming and impressive gateway decorated with animals mi relief the work of a modern egyptian sculptor in the blinding sunlight and among 56 acres of tropical vegetation the animals are kept in open pens which reminded me of regent park the gardens were once the private property of an opulent pasha who it is said built the expensive and unnecessary suspension bridge over an artificial lake because his wife once asked him what a suspension bridge looked like it is fortunate that she never expressed interest in euston station or the arc de triomphe what immediately impressed me about cairo zoo was that the animals were of a size cheerfulness and condition unknown to us in europe i have always for instance considered hippopotamus one of nature more sombre jokes and i have often felt sorry for this great lumbering creature with his vast jaw his swollen body and his small legs the hippopotamus in exile is indeed a sorrowful sight but if you wish to see him looking cheerful and full of surprising vitality you must visit him in africa the hippo in the cairo zoo is a royal beast mighty of muscle with a pinkness under his skin which i take it means perfect health and a wicked and roving little eye other african animals living so happily in their own sunlight prove to a european how the same species deteriorates in northern climates giraffes in europe are poor puny things compared with the huge animals in cairo whose hides are like spotted velour hie ostriches in the cairo zoo are so much at home there that ostrich eggs are sold in the ticket office they cost 2 each what a fuss we make in england if some misguided monkey decides to introduce a baby to our cold climate no publicity agent would like his film star to arrive in london at such a time but in cairo the cages are full of infant monkeys there is a large artificial hill surrounded by a dry moat on which live perhaps 150 baboons they come from west africa there are at this moment at a moderate estimate fifty infant mandrills varying in size from a kitten to a fox terrier these delightful little creatures ride on the backs of their mothers or cling underneath them their puzzled bare little faces peering up through the hair the one tragedy of the cairo zoo is the polar bear although a sympathetic authority has arranged a perpetual cold shower in its cage this poor creature suffers terribly from the heat and should not be in africa at all it is a mangy and pitiable object pointing the moral that wild animals should not be shown outside their native lands which would i suppose defeat the first object of all zoological societies still i wish the miserable bear of cairo could be exchanged for some unhappy hippo from europe the people at the cairo zoo interested me i saw schools of egyptian boys aged about ten dressed in european clothes with the exception of the little red fez or tarbush on each small head these children were just as excited about an elephant ride as little boys are in regents park numerous country sheiks and peasant farmers were wandering round the zoo men who had obviously come up to cairo from the country they would not dream of going to look at the mummies 5i the museum but they were thrilled to see animals such as the crocodile the hippopotamus and the lion with which their predecessors of ancient egypt were more intimately acquainted when they came to some unfamiliar animal they would often smile with pleasure and as i watqfied j them i thought that people who love and understand animals often regard them with affectionate amusement the english are always doing hiis the first books which our children read the animal fantasies like those by beatrix potter in which the humour of the animal characterisation is always delightful because it is based on observation and understanding i am sure that mickey mouse would have been popular in ancient egypt for the people who built the pyramids are the only people of antiquity who recorded the fact that they thought animals amusing and entertaining i some of the most delightful tombs paintings are caricatures one cjf which shows a group of lions start ing back in terror as a stately v domestic cat walks across the road another shows a lion playing chess with a gazelle another shows a jackal paying a visit-to a sick hippopotamus and a third shows a leopard playing a flute to a flock of geese even if the tomb paintings of birds and animals were not so full of life and so obviously the result of loving observation we should know that the ancient egyptians were fond of animals simply on the evidence of these few charming little caricatures the work of some far-off beatrix potter as i watched the modern egyptians in the cairo zoo it seemed to me that they in their love for and amusement in the animals there were touching hands over long centuries with the people who once lived on the banks of the nile

results.fulltext: mr denton lectures ancient egypt mr w denton lectured last night at the oddfellows hall which was fairly filled on ancient egypt its history its monuments and its religion before commencing his lecture he said that ho had been asked if adam waa a pre-historio man if by adam wbb meant the first man he would say then of necessity adam must have been a pre-historic man coming to the subject of bis lecture egypt-wob a country where it almost never rained but portions of which were mo��t fertile through the mud carried down by its single river the nile egypt as the crow flies is about 450 miles long but along the devious course of the nile it measured about 600 miles the delta of the kile equalled one-third of the whole country at one time the inhabitants of egypt numbered 7000000 herethe arts and sciences first flourished and here now rose the grandest monuments in existence geologists told us that in the cretaceous era egypt was covered with water but during the latter part of that era there appeared to have been a gradual rise of the and the lecturer described the geological features of the country and the wild animals that inhabited it before it became the residence of men probably it was first occupied by men immigrating from the west in the stone age j the lecturer in eloquent terms described the gradual steps by which the people arrived at the resolution to transmit to future ages their history by means of the solid pyramids the first king of egypt was believed to have o-eigned about 6000 years ago the lecturer gavo a rapid sketch of the history of the numerous dynasties the three great pjramida belonged to the fourth dynasty tho largest of these covered 13 aores and was 480 feet high it wa�� built of immense blocks of granite brought from a distanco of at least 500 miles it wbb supposed that 100000 men had been employed for sixtysix years in building thia structure the capital of the country was called memphie papyrus books of tho fifth dynasty by far the oldest books with which the world was acquainted could still be road in the museums of paris and other cities the lecturer read extracts from theie books pointing out thoir similarity to passages in the bible reverting to the great pyramid it had often been asked what had caused its erection it would take the whole night merely to enumerate the variou�� theories raised in answer to this question it had been supposed that the pyramids had been raised as barriers against the sand that they had been intended to save people from another general delugo that they had been built by joseph as granaries that they had been halls for freemasons to meet in piazzi smith notions were moro ridiculous still he had supposed tho measures in the various portions of the pyramids to have been divine revelations the people who believed this were those who believed that the english were the descendants of the lost tribes and who were more lost than the tribes themselves laughter there were more than a hundred pyramids of various sizes one 400 feet high in each of which were found either mummies or coffins showing that tbe structuree were intended for tombs the egyptians boueved that in 3000 years tleir bodies would be xe animated and thoy therefore enbalmod their wealthy dead and filled tho i bodies of their poor with asphalt the i lecturer described the means taken to secure j the bodies of the kings from being disturbed in the interior of the pyramids the persians however had broken in to some of the pyramids and had rifled the coffins of their contents tho desire for immortality was as strong within the breast of the egyptian as in that of tho modern christian they were a truly religious nation it was folly to suppose that they worshipped beetles crocodiles kc tbey wero not so stupid but they possessed a religious sentiment the offspring of humanity at a certain stage of its development applause their morality was by no means to be despised the lecturer quoted from egyptian records to show the nature of their moral code their ideas of the deity indicated a groat advance in religion they believed in oneall-poworful god and they prepared during their whole life for the great after death they were to meet what was known of tho history of egypt showed the grot antiquity of man it showed that religion was not the production of any men or of any body of men it showed the necessity for ��bing judgment in matters of religion and it showed how strong was the desire for immortalityin tho human heart tho lecturer in an eloquent peroration spoke of the desirability of an intimate alliance between religion and science aud was loudly applauded as ho retired tho illustrations of tho lecture wore of the uoual excellence to-night mr denton
