results.fulltext: sir william fox on egypt a very large audience assembled last night in the fire brigade hall to listen j to a lecture by sir w fox kcmg on egypt the hall was crowded in every part the chair was taken by mr gilbert carson president of tha tm ca who in introducing the lecturer spoko of the readiness with which sit william fox and the other gentlemen whos lectures had formed part of the winter course had responded to the invitation of the association bir w fox then proceeded to deliver his lecture the opening portion of which was devoted to an explanation of the origin of the recent egyptian difficulty and the causes which had led to armed interference on the part of england and to the suppression of arahi pasha rebellion these causes were connected with the egyptiandebt and the suez canal and as to the former sir william considered that armel interference on the part of england to compel payment of debts due to her subjects was unconstitutional and unjustifiable while with regard to the suez canal it was virtually necessary as her commerce furnished the greater part of the traffic through it that england should take steps to keep the dn-il open and free from damage or 1 disturbance the idea of a canal to connect the bed sea and the mediter anean sir william described as very ancient rameses 11 who flourished 1 2000 years before tbe christian era 1 having constructed one but it was to the genius and perseverance of m de ljflssep�� in faos of a cold reception from the english money market and of the open opposition of lord palmerston 1 that the precent suez canal thehigh-1 waj to british india o wed itsjustence sir wiliam then turned to ancient egypt whioh he desoribed as a land of temples and tombs by the aid of a number of crayon block drawings taken by himself during his travels in egypt he gave a vivid picture of the gigantio temples erected to the ancient goda of the people their vast area and awe-inspiring design and magnitude the beautiful and still undef abed inscriptions and colouring and the impressions which such monuments of the religions of the past produce on the mind of the traveller sir william-devoted a very large portion of his lecture to graphically describing the tombs and burial customs of the egyptians the process by which the bodies of human i beings and even of the animals sacred i to the various gods were converted into mummies in the manner pointed but in i detail by herodotus the father of hisv tory he also dwelt upon the pyramids i which heeonsidered to have-been tombs without doubt and construotedrinthe lifetime of the kings who were buried in them by the labour of hundreds of i thousands of slaves extending overforty i or fifty years with regard to the great pyramid of cheops sir william considered that piazzi smytbe theory i that it was built for astronomical ob ssrvatiohs and that in an inner chamber was the depositary of the divinely re vealed standard of iueasurernenf the multiple of one mch had great probability on its aide and was worthy of careful study he glanced also at the remarkable stone figures known as the sphinxes and the colossi at the obelisks suoh as pompey pillar at alexandria and at the other imperishable remains of a by-gone civilisation whenthousands of years ago arts and sciences schools and writings music poetry and dancing flourished almost as vigorously as in these modern days sir william de scription of some of the domestio customs of the ancient egyptians particularly with regard to their preservation and burial of cats wolves crocodiles and other sacred animals was amusing and interesting the leoturer wonderfully keen powers of insight and observation and his graphic faculty of rapidly describing to an audience what he had himself seen were never displayed to better advantage he briefly pointed out the wayinwhichthe hieroglyphio3 and other forms of egyptian writing that covered all their temples and toniibs and were found recorded in their papyrus had been deciphered in modern times after the world for long centuries had been in utter ignorance of this mode of recording events by means lof pictorial representations of human figures aniinahv and plants he told also how many singular customs of the people and incidents of the historyofr their kings and the practice of their religion worship had been revealed by deciphering the papyrus or egyptian book and sir william created much amusement by reading a letter addressed by an egyptian priest of apis to one of his pupils reproaching him for fre quenting taverns and for breaking a pledge which he had taken to abstain from wine while on the other hand sir william admitted that beer or barley wine was known to the egyptians he pointed out that the mural paintings in the tombs showed that the unferniented juice of the grape i was a beverage used even by the kings the egyptians worshipped bacchus under various other names but in such peculiarly singular estimation was he held that they sacrificed to liim the hog the beast for which of all others they had the deepest aversion in these days said sir w fox we do not sacri fice hogs to bacchus but offer the lives of men by converting them into hogs the remainder of the lecture which though it lasted over two hours was of such deep and sustained interest that the audience would willingly have listened an hour longer was devoted ito anecdotes of rameses 11 cambyses and other kings and conquerors of egypt in conclusion sir william eloquently referred to moses the lawgiver and liberator of his people the greatest of all who ever lived in the land of egypt though not himself an egyptian and brought a niom able lecture to a close by reading bishop alexander splendid 31 lines
